results.title: CentralBankRoBERTa: A fine-tuned large language model ...
results.content: # Research article CentralBankRoBERTa: A fine-tuned large language model for central bank communications☆,. Central bank communications are an important tool for guiding the economy and fulfilling monetary policy goals. Natural language processing (NLP) algorithms have been used to analyze central bank communications. Recent research has introduced deep-learning-based NLP algorithms, also known as large language models (LLMs), which take context into account. This study applies LLMs to central bank communications and constructs CentralBankRoBERTa, a state-of-the-art economic agent classifier that distinguishes five basic macroeconomic agents and binary sentiment classifier that identifies the emotional content of sentences in central bank communications. The absence of large-language models in the central bank communications literature may be attributed to a lack of appropriately labeled datasets. To address this gap, we introduce our model, CentralBankRoBERTa, offering an easy-to-use and standardized tool for scholars of central bank communications. :   We thank Asya Kostanyan, Douglas Laxton, and the participants of the 26th Central Bank Macroeconomic Modeling Workshop for their feedback.

results.title: Using machine learning and big data to analyse the business ...
results.content: **Internet-based data can also help when assessing the tightness of the labour and housing markets.** Analysis for the US labour market shows that including Google-based job-search indicators improves the accuracy of unemployment forecasts, particularly over the medium-term horizon (i.e. three to 12 months ahead).[10] In the euro area, a measure of labour market tightness based on the number of clicks on job postings has recently been built for the Irish economy.[11] For the housing market, analysis for Italy found that metrics based on web-scraped data from an online portal for real estate services can be a leading indicator of housing prices.[12] During the pandemic, Google searches on topics related to job retention schemes and layoffs provided early insight into the strong impact of the pandemic and related policy measures. Following the box entitled “High-frequency data developments in the euro area labour market” in Issue 5/2020 of the ECB’s Economic Bulletin, we conduct a forecasting exercise linking the high-frequency information of the LinkedIn hiring rate to the job finding rate and using the implied path of the aggregate job finding rate as a proxy for the point-in-time, steady-state unemployment rate.

results.title: AI-Based Models for Predicting Financial Crises and ...
results.content: This article provides a comprehensive analysis of AI-based models for predicting financial crises and recessions, examining their methodologies, real-world applications, performance metrics, and future prospects. Recent advances in multi-modal learning have enabled the development of sophisticated crisis prediction systems that simultaneously analyze market data, news sentiment, social media, and network relationships to provide holistic risk assessments. Central banks worldwide have begun incorporating AI-based crisis prediction models into their monetary policy frameworks. Central banks use AI models to continuously monitor systemic risk and identify emerging threats to financial stability. These systems process vast amounts of real-time data from financial markets, banking sectors, and economic indicators to provide comprehensive risk assessments. Banks use AI-based crisis prediction models to enhance their credit risk management frameworks. The evidence from implementations by major central banks, financial institutions, and regulatory agencies demonstrates that AI-based crisis prediction models can deliver significant improvements over traditional approaches.

results.content: Capitalizing on this hypothesis, Sargent and Wallace (Citation1975) extended the analysis, arguing that, as a result of such rational expectations, rule-based monetary policy has no effect on real economic outcomes, unless the central bank has an information advantage over market participants. Elaborating and testing such mitigating strategies is crucial and urgent, as self-fulfilling prophecy dynamics in the monetary policy landscape risk diminishing the ability of central banks to generate policy surprises (Jarociński and Karadi Citation2020), to manage expectations through effective communication and forward guidance, and may, furthermore, limit their ability to deviate from AI-shaped expectations. While most GenAI chatbots are likely to be classified as ‘limited risk’ under existing legal frameworks — for example, under the EU’s AI Act (Brühl Citation2024), the central bank could reasonably argue that oracles forecasting monetary policy outcomes should fall into a higher risk category due to their potential influence on markets, public trust, and macroeconomic dynamics.
